Photograph: Dado Ruvić/Reuters Nvidia Nvidia links with Wall Street firms for $500bn AI financing deal Apollo, BlackRock, Goldman Sachs and KKR among those working with chipmaker to fund infrastructure Reuters Tue 11 Aug 2026 02.32 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Nvidia ⁠has partnered with six major Wall Street financial institutions to raise ⁠more than $500bn (£370bn) capital for artificial intelligence infrastructure. The Nvidia chief executive, Jensen Huang, said on X that the company has ⁠the option to backstop up to $125bn, or 25% of the potential deals. The move highlights how surging demand ⁠for AI computing capacity is drawing institutional investors, as governments, companies and ​startups race to build out ‌datacentres. Big tech companies have signalled that spending on AI ‌would not slow down, with combined outlays set to surpass $730bn this year. However, there has been concerns over the link between high valuations of tech companies and the need for vast investments to support their ambitions . Nvidia signed memorandums of understanding with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR for the financing platforms. The deal will create financing platforms, allowing third-party investors to treat AI “compute” as an asset class. Nvidia, which is worth $5.3tn, counts Google, Amazon, Microsoft and Facebook owner Meta among its customers. “These financing platforms ​will help customers access scarce compute at scale and build the AI factories that will power every industry and country in the age of AI,” Huang said. “Compute has become a critical infrastructure asset,” Joe Bae and Scott Nuttall, the co-chief executives of KKR, said in a joint statement. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Preview latest after newsletter promotion Nvidia said the arrangements would “create dedicated pools of ⁠capital at significant scale at attractive rates” for its customers. The ​company did ​not disclose the financial terms, ​investment commitments by individual firms or a timetable for ​deploying the planned $500bn. Popcorn and Inspiration ‘Madame Curie’: Radiating Resilience This drama tells how a scientist and her husband work together to make great scientific discoveries. Save Mark Us Preferred on Google Print Pierre and Marie Curie in the laboratory, circa 1904 and come to life in a 1943 film. Public Domain Rudolph Lambert Fernandez 7/28/2026 | Updated: 7/28/2026 0:00 X 1 NR | 2 h 4 min | Drama | 1943 Since the early 20th century, the world’s vastly improved understanding and use of radiation has transformed several fields, from medical imaging and cancer therapy to atomic energy. The heavily fictionalized biopic, “Madame Curie,” traces that back to the pioneering 19th-century discovery and study of radium and radioactivity by scientist Marie Curie, and her husband and colleague, Pierre. Impoverished Polish student of physics, chemistry, and mathematics, Marie Sklodowska (Greer Garson) excels at Paris’s University of Sorbonne. Finding her too reclusive for her own good, Prof. Jean Perot (Albert Bassermann) introduces her to a similarly shy, scientifically minded Frenchman, Dr. Pierre Curie (Walter Pidgeon). They conduct their respective experiments in Pierre’s lab. Marie Curie (Greer Garson) in her lab, in "Madame Curie." Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Intrigued by Dr. Henri Becquerel’s (Reginald Owen) discoveries, Marie becomes engrossed in examining how pitchblende gives off rays even independent of the sun. Pierre starts to share her obsession. Lab work blossoms into love, then marriage. Marie gives up her dream of returning to Poland to teach and stays in Paris. Together, they brave the scientific establishment’s prejudice against women leading scientific discovery. Marie braves potentially cancerous burns from prolonged radiation exposure. Through a back-breaking process of trial and error, she discovers a new element: radium. Related Stories ‘Madame Curie’: The Radiance of Shared Discovery Scientists: From the Great to the Lesser Known After four years, having started by processing eight tons of pitchblende, the couple runs over 5,000 sequences of crystallization, distilling out element after element, before isolating radium. They then start to unlock the phenomenal power of radiation. Marie Skłodowska Curie, circa 1920. Public Domain Director Mervyn LeRoy understands the laboratory is a lonely place, prone to silence and seriousness, and wary of impetuousness. Its unglamorous setting, tuned to repeated failure and only rare success, is perfect for the studious, even the socially awkward. Sensitively, he shows how Marie and Pierre, hiding themselves in work, end up finding each other. Poster for "Madame Curie." Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Respect and Warmth Does LeRoy overdo the romance? Perhaps. But he rightly intuits that had there not been a deep bond of respect and warmth between the real-life duo, they couldn’t have collaborated as effectively as they did. He even allows a tinge of humor to lighten the otherwise abidingly grim mood. Once, while toiling away in his dank, drab lab, Pierre presents Marie with one of the first copies of his new book. But with the flourish he lends that gesture, he might as well be brandishing a bouquet. Not to be outdone, Marie reacts as if admiring a fresh cut of flowers. Slowly, she reads out the book’s title: On Symmetry in Physical Phenomena, Symmetry of an Electric Field and of a Magnetic Field. Pierre’s face glows, as if he’s struck a home run. (L–R) Marie Curie (Greer Garson), Jean Perot (Albert Bassermann), Pierre Curie (Walter Pidgeon), and Dr. Becquerel (Reginald Owen), in “Madame Curie.” Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Pidgeon brings his usual gravitas to this performance, reflecting Pierre’s admiration for his wife’s critical thinking, resourcefulness, and eagerness to learn from failure. Garson and her famously upturned eyebrow carry the film by projecting Marie’s spirit of originality alongside her morbid self-doubt and simmering despair. In one scene, Marie is reeling from a shocking turn of events. Garson brings such a sense of devastation to Marie’s bearing, that she sits unblinking, in a single take, for a full four minutes. This is while fellow-actor Bassermann is pacing the room, trying to inspire Marie with an impassioned speech on the virtues of resilience. Unsurprisingly, Garson’s Best Actress Oscar nomination was one of the seven nominations this film secured. Nobel Scientist The real-life Marie was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize, the first person to win a Nobel twice, and the only person to win a Nobel in two distinct sciences: physics and chemistry. The Curies were the first duo to win a Nobel as a married couple. Marie Skłodowska Curie, circa 1920. Public Domain Marie refused to patent their discoveries so that the global scientific community could freely build on their research. Today, radioactivity is measured using the “curie” unit, named in their honor. Good scientists like Thomas Edison or Louis Pasteur become great not by dedicating a mere year or two but by their entire lives to truth-seeking. Importantly, in a speech she delivers here, Marie frames scientific inquiry as a quest for truth. Why does she feel science possesses great beauty? It allows for seemingly inconsequential individuals to grasp an element of truth that, together with what others uncover, reveals a greater, higher truth. Where does science’s “spiritual” strength lie? It lies in its power to cleanse the world of evils: ignorance, wars, poverty, disease. In a plea to her audience of scientists that at once radiates power and humility, Marie urges them to do as she and Pierre had done their whole lives, “Look for the clear light of truth.” You can watch “Madame Curie” on HBOMax, YouTube TV, and Hulu. ‘Madame Curie’ Director: Mervyn LeRoy Starring: Greer Garson, Walter Pidgeon Not Rated Running Time: 2 hours, 4 minutes Release Date: Dec. 15, 1943 Rated: 3 stars out of 5 What arts and culture topics would you like us to cover? https://telex.hu/gazdasag/2026/09/04/mag.text: Menü Kereső Magyar Péter Tiborcz üzleti körének: Vége a közpénzek zabrálásának Gazdaság Madzin Emília Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom A kormány stratégiailag kiemelt jelentőségűvé minősítette a Bayer Construct Zrt. és a ZVK Development Kft. csődeljárását, jelent meg a Magyar Közlönyben péntek este. A Bayer Construct augusztus végén jelentette be, csődeljárást kér maga ellen. A kormány iparpolitikai és gazdasági szempontokat mérlegelve azt állapította meg, hogy meghatározott csődeljárásokban érintett gazdasági szereplők adósságai rendezéséhez és a hitelezőkkel való megegyezéséhez kiemelt gazdaságpolitikai érdek fűződik. Ezzel egyidőben Magyar Péter a Facebookon üzent a Bayernek. „A Bosnyák téri 300 milliárd forintos irodabiznisz kapcsán hadd üzenjem meg innen is Tiborcz Istvánék üzleti körének, azon belül is a Bayer Constructnak és Balázs Attilának. Vége a közpénzek zabrálásának.” „Miután a kormány elállt a szerződésektől, a Bayer Construct és a Bosnyák téri gigaberuházásra létrehozott projektcég, a ZVK Development egymást követő napon csődvédelmet kért. Szeretném bejelenteni, hogy a Tisza-kormány válaszul stratégiailag kiemelt jelentőségűvé minősítette a Bayer Construct Zrt. és a ZVK Development Kft. csődeljárását. A magyar állam kitettsége ezen cégek kapcsán messze túlmutat az egyetlen Bosnyák téri beruházáson. A Magyar Fejlesztési Bank közvetlen és közvetett kitettsége a Bayer-csoporttal szemben mintegy 207 milliárd forint közpénz” – mondta a miniszterelnök. Magyar azzal folytatta, hogy a kormány a két csődeljárásban a kizárólag állami tulajdonban álló Nemzeti Reorganizációs Nonprofit Kft.-t rendelte ki vagyonfelügyelőként. Az állami vagyonfelügyelő transzparensen áttekintheti a cégek teljes vagyoni helyzetét, betekinthet a könyveikbe, megvizsgálhatja a szerződéseiket és a pénzforgalmi számláikat, valamint ellenőrizheti az új kötelezettségvállalásaikat. A cégek a vagyonfelügyelő jóváhagyása nélkül új vagyoni kötelezettséget nem vállalhatnak, az engedélye nélkül kötött ügyleteket pedig megtámadhatja, és a csődvédelem szabályaiba ütköző kifizetések visszakövetelését kezdeményezheti. Ha pedig korábbi vagyonkimentés gyanúját észleli, azt köteles a bíróságnak és az illetékes hatóságoknak bejelenteni. A vagyonkezelő feladata lesz a hitelezői követelések nyilvántartása, és a hitelezőkkel kötendő egyezség előkészítésének ellenőrzése is. „Erre azért van szükség, mert ilyen mértékű állami kitettség és egy ilyen időzítésű csődhelyzet mellett valós és súlyos kockázatként kell számolnunk a vagyon esetleges kimenekítésével. A célunk világos. Minden rendelkezésünkre álló törvényes eszközzel megakadályozzuk, hogy a tulajdonosok vagy a mögöttük álló személyek vagyont menekítsenek ki a cégekből, miközben a veszteséget az államra, a hitelezőkre, a dolgozókra és az alvállalkozókra hagynák. Szeretném innen is emlékeztetni Tiborcz István üzlettársát, a Bayer Construct tulajdonosát, a fizetésképtelenséget fenyegető helyzetben lévő gazdálkodó szervezet vagyonának elvonása, színlelt ügyletek megkötése, csődbűncselekmény. Nem fogjuk hagyni, hogy következmények nélkül maradjon, ha megkárosítják a magyar államot és az adófizetőket” – mondta a miniszterelnök. Csütörtökön a zuglói képviselő-testület bejelentette, hogy pert indítanak a Bayer-csoport ellen a Bosnyák téri irodakomplexum ügyében. Az irodakomplexumot Balázs Attila cégei húzták fel, annak megvásárlására pedig még az előző kormány kötött nettó 244 milliárdos, később nettó 254,8 milliárdosra módosított szerződést. Az állam és a Bayer közötti jogi hercehurcáról ebben a cikkben írtunk részletesen . Ha az államnak sikerül elállnia az irodaházak megvásárlásától, akkor a Bayernek piaci vevőnek kell majd eladnia őket, ezt nehezítheti meg a zuglói önkormányzat pere, kérdés ugyanis, hogy találnak-e olyan befektetőt, aki megvenné a perrel érintett ingatlanokat. Bayer Construct és a ZVK Development azután kezdeményezte a csődeljárást, hogy a Tisza-kormány augusztus 3-án bejelentette , eláll a Zuglói Városközpont névre keresztelt gigaprojekt megvásárlásától, és 300 milliárd forintot követelnek vissza. Magyar Péter ekkor azt mondta, a Magyar Nemzeti Vagyonkezelő (MNV) a jogi átvilágítás közben számos szerződésszegést állapított meg, a zárási feltételek közel fele nem teljesült, az ingatlanokat továbbra is terhelte a zuglói önkormányzat elővásárlási joga, pedig ezt a zárás előtt töröltetni kellett volna. A kormány érve szerint az állam erre hivatkozva állhat el jogszerűen az ügylettől, és követelheti vissza a már kifizetett részleteket, a foglaló kétszeresét, valamint kötbért és adott esetben kártérítést is. A csődeljárás bejelentése után úgy tűnt, hogy a Bayer részéről ez egy jól megtervezett stratégiai lépés volt, amivel időt nyerhet az állammal szemben. A Bayer Construct körül kialakult helyzetről, az épülő lakások sorsáról és a csődeljárás részleteiről ebben a cikkben írtunk. Kedvenceink Partnereinktől Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! My application remains “under consideration”.’ Photograph: Alamy View image in fullscreen ‘Five months later, and over £7,000 on costs, I am still waiting. My application remains “under consideration”.’ Photograph: Alamy Home Office Letters A painful truth about post-Brexit immigration While the media rightly highlights the harsh treatment of UK citizens abroad, the UK Home Office is quietly inflicting similar cruelty, says Vera-Lynn Watson Sun 13 Sep 2026 11.54 EDT Last modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 11.56 EDT Share Your report ( Wife of British man at risk of deportation from Sweden calls on Burnham to intervene, 3 September ) highlights a painful truth about post-Brexit immigration: families are being treated as administrative burdens rather than human beings. However, this harsh treatment cuts both ways. I am a 71-year-old German-American citizen, married to my British husband for 38 years. We have only ever been apart for work. We bought property in the UK in 2023 so my husband could retire there. After retiring from my job in Germany, I applied for a UK family visa on 1 April 2026, expecting to settle down with him and my two adult sons within six weeks. The lawyer was rather optimistic. Five months later, and over £7,000 on costs, I am still waiting. My application remains “under consideration”. I have hired a lawyer, involved an MP, filed official complaints, and paid for priority services, yet the Home Office remains an impenetrable wall. While British media rightly highlights the harsh treatment of UK citizens abroad, the UK Home Office is quietly inflicting the exact same cruelty on older spouses from allied nations. At 71, my husband and I are losing precious time together to bureaucratic inertia. If we expect European countries to show humanity to British citizens, the UK must show the same decency to the families of its own people. Vera-Lynn Watson Birkenfeld, Germany Explore more on these topics Home Office Immigration and asylum Brexit European Union Europe letters Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text: Wes Streeting, defence secretary, inspects the equipment used by Rheinmetall to produce large-calibre weapons. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Wes Streeting, defence secretary, inspects the equipment used by Rheinmetall to produce large-calibre weapons. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian Manufacturing sector Race to rearm: Telford gun hall brings tank barrel production back to the UK Defence secretary says Britain must manufacture at scale as Germany’s Rheinmetall opens Midlands factory Jasper Jolly Thu 22 Oct 2026 12.59 EDT Last modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 13.44 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google F or the last 20 years, Britain was unable to put a barrel on its tanks without buying from abroad. Relying on foreign allies seemed like a reasonable choice during years of relative security (for wealthy countries at least) after the end of the cold war. But Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 has changed the calculation – and prompted a scramble to rearm among European countries, including the UK. Evidence of that scramble was on display on Thursday in Shropshire, where the UK defence secretary, Wes Streeting , opened a factory hastily constructed by Germany’s Rheinmetall to make barrels for artillery and British tanks. Such was the urgency that Rheinmetall’s chief executive, Armin Papperger, said the company had started investment “off the back of a handshake” before Christmas last year with Gen Sir Roly Walker, who leads the British army as chief of the general staff, without waiting for a formal contract. Eight months later, production of the first barrels at the factory in Telford has started. Papperger said he was in talks to produce more ammunition in the UK as well, with a decision due in the next six to eight months. Streeting said: “It is not enough to simply out-innovate those who would wish us harm – though we must. We must also out-produce them too. Because advantage increasingly belongs to those who can manufacture at scale and field the capability fastest.” View image in fullscreen From left: Armin Papperger, chief executive of Rheinmetall, Wes Streeting and Gen Sir Roly Walker. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian The factory takes a 3.2 tonne, 8-metre cylinder of specialised steel alloy and drills a hole through it to make the barrel shape. The surfaces are then honed to remove imperfections, before another turning tool adds spiral rifling to add to artillery accuracy. A specialised machine – one of only two in the world – increases the pressure inside the barrel to about 15,000 times the air at sea level to harden it for the explosive power needed to propel shells as far as 30km (18 miles). The Ukraine war will go down in history as the moment when militaries woke up to the brutal new reality of drone warfare . But for all the focus on uncrewed weapons, Walker said they cannot rival more traditional armaments for sheer firepower. “In Ukraine , we know that both sides fire tens of thousands of rounds of artillery ammunition every day, and that generates a weight of fire and levels of lethality across the battlefield that drones alone cannot replicate,” said Walker, in a speech at the factory opening. He said it had been “sad” when the UK was unable to continue centuries of artillery manufacture that had lasted through the Napoleonic wars, two world wars and the cold war. Much of that work was carried out at the Royal Arsenal in Woolwich, which opened in the 17th century (and whose workers set up a football club that moved to north London in 1913). Yet production ceased in 1967, with the work scattered first around the country and then in some cases moving abroad. The new Telford gun hall will bring that capability back to the UK, albeit starting with production for guns for German-made, self-propelled, remote-control howitzers that take Nato-standard 155mm ammunition. However, in the future it will also be able to make slightly smaller tank barrels that use 120mm rounds. These include the Challenger 3 tank, which is now going through final testing, and a British version of the remote-control howitzer planned for after May 2028. View image in fullscreen Gen Sir Roly Walker, chief of the defence staff, peers down a 155mm artillery barrel during a tour of the new gun hall in Telford. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian The factory will be able to make 245 barrels a year, plus 50 breeches – the part at the base of the barrel – although Papperger said annual capacity could theoretically be expanded to as much as 1,000 within four or five years, but only if the orders came in. Exports may also be on the agenda. Papperger added that Nato allies could manage with smaller output than Russia and its client states because of their higher quality. A Russian barrel will be able to fire about 500 times before breaking, while the products from Telford should survive as many as 4,000 shots, he said. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning after newsletter promotion Royal Navy lacks resources to counter Russian threat in high north, MPs warn Read more The Telford investment followed an agreement in 2024 between Keir Starmer, then prime minister, and his German counterpart, Olaf Scholz. It was part of a wide-ranging pact for the two largest military spenders in Europe to work together more closely. Rheinmetall employs about 685 people in Telford, although only 35 will work in the gun hall, rising to 100 when it is at full capacity – hardly enough to kickstart the “reindustrialisation” of Britain desired by Andy Burnham. The bulk of the workers in Telford make the Challenger and Boxer armoured vehicles in a joint venture with Britain’s key arms maker, BAE Systems. Rheinmetall has been among the biggest beneficiaries of the massive increase in European spending on defence and in supplying arms to Ukraine. US intelligence services in 2024 reportedly foiled a Russian plot to assassinate Papperger in apparent retaliation against the company’s production of weapons for Kyiv. The German company’s market value has risen from about €4.2bn (£3.5bn) in the days before Russia’s invasion to €47bn on Wednesday, though it has dropped back from a peak of nearly double that last year. Rheinmetall and other European defence companies, including BAE Systems and the British jet engine maker Rolls-Royce, have benefited particularly from European governments eager to reduce reliance on the US arms industry at a time when the White House has shown itself willing to divert supplies to its own militaries ahead of allies. Papperger said more governments were saying they wanted control over their weapons production. That could help to mollify Donald Trump, the US president, who has shown himself willing to undermine previously firm alliances. “To be a strong partner, you need strong armies,” said Papperger. “But on the other side, you need a strong industry. And this is what we do at the moment. We build up the industry.” Explore more on these topics Manufacturing sector Defence policy British army Weapons technology Telford Military Wes Streeting features Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Make NHS and military uniforms in UK, fashion firms urge Burnham UK manufacturing growth picks up as Trump tariff chaos eases Listen to manufacturers and unions: high electricity prices are killing industry Britain ‘faces deindustrialisation’ without relief from high energy prices, survey warns UK economy shrank by 0.1% in April as Iran war held back growth UK poised to ease steel tariffs as manufacturers warn of costs Rolls-Royce secures nearly £600m in UK government cash to develop small reactors Centuries-old pottery firm Denby set to call in administrators UK car production falls 17% as industry warns of ‘worrying’ decline UK manufacturers hit by sharpest rise in cost inflation since Black Wednesday in 1992 Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.politico.eu/article/france-v.text: PARIS — Lawmakers in the French National Assembly will vote on a Socialist Party proposal to grant amnesty to an estimated 300,000 to 400,000 unauthorized immigrants employed in France. The measure is expected to be supported by center-left presidential candidate Raphaël Glucksmann, whose campaign is eager to find some breathing space between centrist candidates like Gabriel Attal and Edouard Philippe, and Jean-Luc Mélenchon, his rival on the radical left. Glucksmann has previously expressed support for such a step in multiple interviews. The proposal , introduced by Socialist lawmaker Paul Christophle, hails Spain’s Pedro Sánchez for having “chosen to provide foreign nationals with the legal means to settle and work” instead of “trying — in vain — to control migration flows.” Advertisement Advertisement Earlier this year , Spain moved to grant legal status to half a million unauthorized immigrants who could prove they had been living in Spain for at least five months, could provide proof of employment or a familial link to the country and did not have a criminal record. Christophle wants to grant legal status to an estimated 300,000 to 400,000 people who have been employed in France for over six months but without proper documentation. The bill is likely to unite left-leaning MPs in the French National Assembly, but opposition from center-right and far-right groups means it will probably fail. However, Glucksmann’s campaign hopes the proposal will highlight a rift between lawmakers backing French President Emmanuel Macron and voters who elected him in 2022 — some of whom are more progressive on issues like immigration. The debate on immigration will be an effective way to differentiate Glucksmann from his center-right rival Édouard Philippe, who believes that amnesty plans should be contingent on a European agreement, said an official who is backing the center-left MEP. It might also help poach Macron voters “who are completely opposed to a closed society,” he added. Among those who voted for Macron in 2022, 29% plan to vote for Raphaël Glucksmann next year, according to a Cluster17 poll commissioned by POLITICO , against 49% for Édouard Philippe. Glucksmann is currently projected to receive 13% of the overall vote, according to the poll, against 16% for Philippe. They both trail far-right frontrunner Marine Le Pen (33%) and Mélenchon (18.5%). The top two candidates will advance to a runoff if no one wins a majority in the first round. The bill is scheduled to be voted on Nov. 19. Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.digi24.ro/stiri/externe/casa.text: Casa Albă a confirmat oficial vineri că un summit fără precedent între preşedinţii american Donald Trump, chinez Xi Jinping şi rus Vladimir Putin va avea loc joia viitoare în China, având pe agendă cel mai probabil războiul din Orientul Mijlociu, dar nu şi cel din Ucraina, relatează AFP şi dpa, potrivit Agerpres. Reuniunea, care a fost un subiect de discuţie timp de săptămâni întregi fără a fi confirmată, va avea loc în marja summitului Cooperării Economice Asia-Pacific (APEC) de la Shenzhen, în sudul Chinei. Evenimentul va marca o nouă etapă în revenirea lui Vladimir Putin - izolat de statele occidentale de la invadarea Ucrainei în 2022 - pe scena internaţională, având loc la puţin peste un an de la întâlnirea sa cu Donald Trump în Alaska. Nici Beijingul, nici Moscova nu au confirmat oficial reuniunea, deşi au lăsat să se înţeleagă în ultimele săptămâni că astfel de discuţii ar putea avea loc. Posibilele subiecte de discuţie dintre liderii celor trei puteri dotate cu arme nucleare sunt numeroase şi, deşi este puţin probabil ca summitul să aducă rezultate concrete, va fi cu siguranţă prilejul unei fotografii istorice, notează AFP. „Preşedintele a precizat clar că intenţionează să abordeze, printre altele, problema reducerii numărului de arme nucleare la nivel mondial. Preşedintele Trump consideră că această proliferare este extrem de periculoasă”, a declarat vineri seară pentru presă, Olivia Wales purtătoarea de cuvânt a Casei Albe. „Cred că preşedintele are intenţia de a ridica problema Iranului în timpul reuniunii trilaterale cu Xi Jinping şi Vladimir Putin”, a adăugat un oficial american, sub protecţia anonimatului, în cadrul unei conferinţe telefonice cu media. Acesta a menţionat că Washingtonul urmează o „cale complet separată” de negocieri cu Kievul şi Moscova, precizând că Beijingul „nu face parte propriu-zis din acest proces”. Prin urmare, nu pare oportună abordarea chestiunii Ucrainei, a conchis el. Urmărește știrile Digi24.ro și pe Google News
